blocks.text: Given a number n, decide whether it is an ugly number, meaning its only prime factors are 2, 3, and 5. By convention, 1 counts as ugly, and any number that is 0 or negative does not.

blocks.title: Analogy: Sorting Groceries Into Only Three Baskets
blocks.text: Picture unpacking a crate of items and sorting every item into one of exactly three baskets: a basket for pairs, a basket for triples, and a basket for groups of five. If every single item in the crate fits neatly into one of those three baskets with nothing left over, the crate is "ugly" in this problem's sense. If even one item does not belong in any of the three baskets, like a group of seven, the crate fails the sort.

blocks.caption: Strip out every factor of 2, 3, and 5, and see what is left

blocks.text: 1 is considered ugly by definition, with an empty factor chain, since it has no prime factors at all to check.
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what "only built from 2, 3, and 5" really means.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every number can be broken down into its prime factors, and an ugly number is defined entirely by which primes are allowed to appear in that breakdown.

Observation 2: If every copy of the factors 2, 3, and 5 is divided out completely, whatever number remains represents everything else the original number was built from.

Observation 3: If that remainder is exactly 1, nothing outside the allowed set of 2, 3, and 5 was ever present, so the number is ugly. If it is anything else, some other prime factor exists.

Observation 4: Since only three fixed factors ever need checking, and each division shrinks the number quickly, this check can stop early the moment the number reaches 1, since nothing left to check could change the answer at that point.
That reasoning alone already sketches the whole solution: strip the three allowed factors completely, and see if exactly 1 is left.

The most direct approach is to strip every factor of 2, then every factor of 3, then every factor of 5 out of n, dividing each one out completely before moving to the next. Whatever remains at the end reveals whether n was ugly.

items: If n is 0 or negative, return false immediately.
While n is divisible by 2, divide it by 2.
While n is divisible by 3, divide it by 3.
While n is divisible by 5, divide it by 5.
If n has been reduced all the way to 1, it is ugly, otherwise it is not.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: strip out 2s, then 3s, then 5s, one factor family at a time

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The n <= 0 check happens first, as a dedicated rejection, since the factor-stripping loop has no natural way to reject zero or negative numbers on its own.

Each factor uses its own while loop, not a single if check, specifically because a number can contain the same prime factor multiple times, like 32 containing five copies of 2, and every copy needs to be removed.
The three factors are checked in a fixed order, 2 then 3 then 5, though the order among these three specific factors does not actually affect correctness, only convention and readability.

blocks.text: This works because dividing out every copy of 2, then every copy of 3, then every copy of 5, removes exactly the allowed prime factors. Whatever is left over must be built from some other prime, which immediately disqualifies n.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n), since each division shrinks n, and there are at most log base 2, log base 3, and log base 5 of n divisions combined.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: this solution already reaches a very good complexity, since it is bounded purely by how many times n can be repeatedly divided. The remaining opportunity is mostly about writing it more cleanly, with an early exit once n reaches 1, rather than continuing to check factors that can no longer matter.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking all three factors in every case works but is not fully necessary: once n has already been reduced to 1, none of the remaining factor checks can possibly change the outcome.

What the wasted checks cost: a small, bounded number of modulo operations against factors that no longer apply, not a change in complexity class, just avoidable work.

Can the loop recognize when nothing more can change: yes, checking whether n equals 1 right after fully stripping out each factor tells us exactly that.

What should happen the moment that is detected: stop checking the remaining factors immediately, there is nothing left they could possibly affect.

The core idea: strip each factor completely, but break out of the loop early the instant n reaches 1.

Once n has been reduced to 1, none of the remaining factor checks can change the answer, so there is no reason to keep testing them. Looping over the three factors and breaking out early the moment n hits 1 avoids that small amount of wasted work.
This does not change the complexity class, since the loop was already efficient, but it does avoid unnecessary modulo checks on factors that no longer apply.
Loop through the factors 2, 3, and 5 in order. For each one, divide it out of n completely. As soon as n reaches 1, stop checking the remaining factors early.

blocks.text: n reaches 1 after only two divisions, and the factor 5 never needs to be checked at all, confirming 6 is ugly.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: divide out each factor completely, exit as soon as n reaches 1

blocks.text: This works because stripping out every copy of 2, then every copy of 3, then every copy of 5 is mathematically identical to the brute force version, the early exit only changes when the loop stops, never what it computes. Once n has been reduced to 1, no further division by 3 or 5 could ever change n away from 1, since dividing 1 by anything larger than 1 never divides evenly, so continuing to check those factors is guaranteed to be wasted work, not a source of a different answer.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["n reaches 1 during factor stripping","The loop breaks immediately, skipping any remaining factors","True, ugly number"],["n never reaches 1 after all three factors are stripped","Some other prime factor remains in n, disqualifying it","False, not an ugly number"]]}

items: The break statement sits immediately after the n == 1 check, right after each factor's own while loop finishes, so it only ever skips factors that have not been checked yet, never the one currently being processed.

Checking n == 1 after each factor, not just once at the very end, is what allows the early exit to trigger as soon as possible, rather than always running through all three factors regardless of whether n has already reached 1.
The final return n == 1 is unchanged from the brute force version, since the early exit only affects how quickly the loop gets there, not what condition determines the final answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n), the same order as the brute force, but with fewer wasted checks once n reaches 1 early.
Space: O(1). Since only three fixed factors are ever checked and each division shrinks n exponentially fast, this is already effectively optimal, there is no further complexity class to reach.

blocks.text: The core pattern here is systematically stripping out allowed prime factors and checking what remains. This same "divide out the allowed factors one at a time" idea reappears in other problems about numbers built from a restricted set of primes, like problems asking for the n-th ugly number.

items: Forgetting to reject n = 0 and negative numbers before running the factor stripping loop.
Checking the factors with if instead of while, which only removes one copy of each factor instead of all of them.
Assuming a number is ugly just because it is divisible by 2, 3, or 5 once, rather than checking that nothing else is left over.

blocks.text: This problem is often a stepping stone toward harder "ugly number" variants, like generating the n-th ugly number in order. Being comfortable with the factor stripping idea here builds directly toward those follow up problems, worth mentioning if asked what comes next.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid unnecessary checks", think: break out of the factor loop the moment n reaches 1.
If the interviewer says "what if a factor appears more than once", think: use a while loop per factor, not an if, to strip every copy.
If the interviewer says "what comes next after this problem", think: generating the n-th ugly number in order, which builds directly on this same factor idea.

items: Why must each factor be stripped with a while loop instead of a single if check?
Can you generate the n-th ugly number in increasing order, building on this same idea?
How would the approach change if the allowed prime factors were a different, possibly larger, set of primes?
Does the order in which the three factors, 2, 3, and 5, are checked affect correctness or only performance?
What is the largest number of times any single factor could need to be divided out for a valid 32 bit integer input?
The n-th ugly number problem, which builds directly on this same factor-restriction idea using a min-heap or dynamic programming approach.
Any "is this number built only from an allowed set of primes" problem, which reuses the exact same strip-each-factor-completely technique.
Prime factorization problems in general, where systematically dividing out each candidate factor reveals a number's complete structure.
Early-exit optimizations in loops more broadly, recognizing the exact moment remaining iterations cannot change the outcome, and stopping there.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The straightforward factor stripping approach already runs in O(log n) time and O(1) space. Adding an early exit once n reaches 1 avoids some wasted checks in practice, but does not change the underlying complexity class, since the factor stripping itself was already the efficient approach from the start.

items: Pattern: systematically stripping out a restricted set of allowed prime factors, 2, 3, and 5, and checking what remains.
Core Idea: divide out every copy of each allowed factor completely; if exactly 1 remains, no other prime factor was ever present, so the number is ugly.
Time: O(log n) for both versions shown here.
Space: O(1) for both.
Most Important Observation: this problem is already efficient in its most direct form, the only real refinement available is stopping early once nothing left could change the answer.
Interview Difficulty: easy to solve correctly, but this problem is often a stepping stone toward harder ugly-number variants like generating the n-th ugly number.
One line memory trick: strip out 2s, 3s, and 5s completely, if only 1 remains, it is ugly.
